The latter will have vectors that look like νi=mi′+νr\nu_{i}=m_{i}^{\prime}+\nu_{r} where 0≠mi′∈𝒱r−10\neq m_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}_{r-1}. Because of the partitioning, |ℳ|+1+|𝒩|=D|\mathcal{M}|+1+|\mathcal{N}|=D. Note any future use of mi,mi′m_{i},m_{i}^{\prime} will refer to a νi\nu_{i} inside ℳ,𝒩\mathcal{M},\mathcal{N} respectively. We emphasize that ℳ,𝒩\mathcal{M},\mathcal{N} are sets and not necessarily a linear subspace.

We would like to invent a new set of DD vectors with rank r−1r-1, so that we can apply the induction hypothesis. To do so, let us replace νr\nu_{r} with some l∈𝒱r−1l\in\mathcal{V}_{r-1}, and similarly substitute every νr\nu_{r} in the linear expansion of any νi=mi′+νr∈𝒩\nu_{i}=m_{i}^{\prime}+\nu_{r}\in\mathcal{N}, meaning νi\nu_{i} becomes l+mi′l+m_{i}^{\prime}. This vector ll needs to satisfy some properties:

l≠𝟎,mi′+l≠𝟎,\displaystyle l\neq\bm{0},m_{i}^{\prime}+l\neq\bm{0}, (50)
l≠mj,mi′+l≠mj\displaystyle l\neq m_{j},m_{i}^{\prime}+l\neq m_{j} (51)

The first two conditions ensure that after replacement, we do not obtain any zero vector. The second line ensures that we do not obtain any repeated vector. All these conditions amount to l∉{𝟎,mi′,mj,mj+mi′}l\not\in\{\bm{0},m_{i}^{\prime},m_{j},m_{j}+m_{i}^{\prime}\}, the size of this set being (at most) 1+|𝒩|+|ℳ|+|ℳ|⋅|𝒩|1+|\mathcal{N}|+|\mathcal{M}|+|\mathcal{M}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|. We recall 1+|𝒩|+|ℳ|=D1+|\mathcal{N}|+|\mathcal{M}|=D, so the size is ≤D+(D−1−|𝒩|)​|𝒩|≤D+D2/4≤2log⁡D+22​log⁡D−2<2r−1=22​log⁡D−t−2\leq D+(D-1-|\mathcal{N}|)|\mathcal{N}|\leq D+D^{2}/4\leq 2^{\log D}+2^{2\log D-2}<2^{r-1}=2^{2\log D-t-2} as t>1t>1. Hence, there exists l∈𝒱r−1l\in\mathcal{V}_{r-1} that satisfies Eqs. 50 and 51.

Now the induction hypothesis for the new set of DD vectors apply, since the rank has clearly been decreased by one to r−1=2​log⁡D−1+t−1r-1=2\log D-1+t-1. Therefore, there exists a subspace 𝒲=span​⟨w1,…,wt−1⟩⊂𝒱r−1\mathcal{W}=\text{span}\langle w_{1},\ldots,w_{t-1}\rangle\subset\mathcal{V}_{r-1} satisfying Eq. 49 for this new set of vectors. Now let us bring back νr\nu_{r} by undoing the replacement by ll. After this change, we need to verify that 𝒲\mathcal{W} still satisfies Eq. 49, and then, in order to finish the proof, extend 𝒲\mathcal{W} by a vector wtw_{t} while satisfying said properties. We verify the properties as follows:

  • •

    We first check that νi,νi+νj∉𝒲\nu_{i},\nu_{i}+\nu_{j}\not\in\mathcal{W}. Note that νi∉𝒲\nu_{i}\not\in\mathcal{W} needs to be checked only for νr\nu_{r} and νi∈𝒩\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{N} (as they are the only ones impacted by bringing back νr\nu_{r}). For both, this is in fact obvious as ({νr}∪𝒩)⊂𝒱r−𝒱r−1⟹({νr}∪𝒩)∩𝒱r−1=∅(\{\nu_{r}\}\cup\mathcal{N})\subset\mathcal{V}_{r}-\mathcal{V}_{r-1}\implies(\{\nu_{r}\}\cup\mathcal{N})\cap\mathcal{V}_{r-1}=\emptyset while 𝒲⊂𝒱r−1\mathcal{W}\subset\mathcal{V}_{r-1}.

  • •

    For the property νi+νj∉𝒲\nu_{i}+\nu_{j}\not\in\mathcal{W}, this needs to be checked only when at least one of νi,νj\nu_{i},\nu_{j} is inside ({νr}∪𝒩)(\{\nu_{r}\}\cup\mathcal{N}).

    • –

      Assume that νi∈({νr}∪𝒩)\nu_{i}\in(\{\nu_{r}\}\cup\mathcal{N}) and νj=mj∈ℳ\nu_{j}=m_{j}\in\mathcal{M}. If νi=νr\nu_{i}=\nu_{r}, we need to show νr+mj∉𝒲\nu_{r}+m_{j}\not\in\mathcal{W} and for νi∈𝒩\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{N}, we need to prove mi′+νr+mj∉𝒲m_{i}^{\prime}+\nu_{r}+m_{j}\not\in\mathcal{W}. Both these cases, due to νr\nu_{r}, are outside of 𝒱r−1\mathcal{V}_{r-1} and 𝒲⊂𝒱r−1\mathcal{W}\subset\mathcal{V}_{r-1}.

    • –

      Assume that νi,νj∈({νr}∪𝒩)\nu_{i},\nu_{j}\in(\{\nu_{r}\}\cup\mathcal{N}). Then we need to check νr+mj′+νr=mj′∉𝒲\nu_{r}+m_{j}^{\prime}+\nu_{r}=m_{j}^{\prime}\not\in\mathcal{W}, and also mi′+νr+mj′+νr=mi′+mj′∉𝒲m_{i}^{\prime}+\nu_{r}+m_{j}^{\prime}+\nu_{r}=m_{i}^{\prime}+m_{j}^{\prime}\not\in\mathcal{W}. However by induction hypothesis, we already know that l+mj′+l=mj′∉𝒲l+m_{j}^{\prime}+l=m_{j}^{\prime}\not\in\mathcal{W} and l+mi′+l+mj′=mi′+mj′∉𝒲l+m_{i}^{\prime}+l+m_{j}^{\prime}=m_{i}^{\prime}+m_{j}^{\prime}\not\in\mathcal{W}, so this is also guaranteed.

Finally, we need to find a new wtw_{t} to add to 𝒲\mathcal{W} while preserving its properties. Let us define wt=νr+lw_{t}=\nu_{r}+l and let 𝒲′=𝒲⊕wt⊂𝒱r=𝒱r−1⊕νr\mathcal{W}^{\prime}=\mathcal{W}\oplus w_{t}\subset\mathcal{V}_{r}=\mathcal{V}_{r-1}\oplus\nu_{r}. To prove that 𝒲′\mathcal{W}^{\prime} satisfies Eq. 49, one needs to verify that νi∉𝒲′−𝒲\nu_{i}\not\in\mathcal{W}^{\prime}-\mathcal{W} or νi−νj∉𝒲′−𝒲\nu_{i}-\nu_{j}\not\in\mathcal{W}^{\prime}-\mathcal{W}, as 𝒲\mathcal{W} has already been shown to satisfy said properties. If νi∈𝒲′−𝒲\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{W}^{\prime}-\mathcal{W} or νi−νj∈𝒲′−𝒲\nu_{i}-\nu_{j}\in\mathcal{W}^{\prime}-\mathcal{W} then wtw_{t} must be ‘involved’:

  • •

    For νi∈𝒲′−𝒲\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{W}^{\prime}-\mathcal{W}, we must have νi=wt+w=νr+l+w\nu_{i}=w_{t}+w=\nu_{r}+l+w for some w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, in which case νi−l=νr+w\nu_{i}-l=\nu_{r}+w. However, the latter is inside 𝒱r−𝒱r−1\mathcal{V}_{r}-\mathcal{V}_{r-1}. Therefore, since l∈𝒱r−1l\in\mathcal{V}_{r-1}, we have νi∈𝒱r−𝒱r−1\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{r}-\mathcal{V}_{r-1}. So νi∈({νr}∪N)\nu_{i}\in(\{\nu_{r}\}\cup N). If νi=νr\nu_{i}=\nu_{r} then l=w∈𝒲l=w\in\mathcal{W}, which violates our induction hypothesis. If νi=mi′+νr∈N\nu_{i}=m_{i}^{\prime}+\nu_{r}\in N then mi′+l=w∈𝒲m_{i}^{\prime}+l=w\in\mathcal{W}, which again violates the construction of 𝒲\mathcal{W}.

  • •

    For νi−νj=νr+l+w\nu_{i}-\nu_{j}=\nu_{r}+l+w for some w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, exactly one of νi\nu_{i} or νj\nu_{j} must be inside ({νr}∪N)(\{\nu_{r}\}\cup N). Without loss of generality assume νi=νr\nu_{i}=\nu_{r} or νi=mi′+νr\nu_{i}=m_{i}^{\prime}+\nu_{r}. Then this simplifies to l−νj=w∈𝒲l-\nu_{j}=w\in\mathcal{W} or mi′+l−νj=w∈𝒲m_{i}^{\prime}+l-\nu_{j}=w\in\mathcal{W}, both violating the induction hypothesis for 𝒲\mathcal{W}.

This shows 𝒲′\mathcal{W}^{\prime} satisfies Eq. 49 and finishes the induction. The significant cost in each inductive step is the search to find ll, taking O⁡(D2/2+D)O(D^{2}/2+D) steps.

Resource estimation. The total complexity is found by applying this for each induction step, thus O⁡(t​D2)O(tD^{2}). Note that t≤min⁡(2​N,D)−2​log⁡D+1t\leq\min(2N,D)-2\log D+1, with equality when all the vectors νi\nu_{i} are linearly independent; so the total cost of the classical algorithm used to find UU is at most O⁡(D2​(min⁡(2​N,D)−2​log⁡D+1))O(D^{2}(\min(2N,D)-2\log D+1)). It should be noted that the search process can be fully parallelized, using all cores on an available machine, and given the nature of this search, the expected runtime could be much less. ∎

Appendix D Trading off Toffolis with qubits in the SOS algorithm

As explained in the main text, trading off Toffolis with qubits can be done by using an alternative version of QROM. This variant, which we shall call SelSwapDirty [68, Fig. 1d], has a parameter λ\lambda that allows for trading off qubits with Toffolis. For a QROM loading LL many data points |xi⟩\left|x_{i}\right\rangle, indexed by i=1,…,Li=1,\ldots,L and of size cc, the trade-off λ∈[1,L]\lambda\in[1,L] can be applied to change the Toffoli complexity from O⁡(L)O(L) to O⁡(L/λ+λ​c)O(L/\lambda+\lambda c) while increasing the uninitialized (so-called dirty) qubit cost to O⁡(λ​c)O(\lambda c). Notice that the volume cost stays as O⁡(L​c)O(Lc), although technically, as we traded gates with dirty qubits, this volume is not a clean volume, so it is an overall improvement. To keep our discussion focused on the novelties and following the convention in previous resource estimations [69], we will select λ=L/c\lambda=\sqrt{L/c} in our applications. This strikes a balance in the trade off, using ‘equally’ many (O⁡(L​c)O(\sqrt{Lc})) Toffolis as dirty qubits.

The first expensive QROM is employed when outputting the system register in Eq. 10. Using the SelSwapDirty variant with Toffoli cost 2​D/λ+8​(2​N)​λ2D/\lambda+8(2N)\lambda with λ=2​D/16​N\lambda=\sqrt{2D/16N}, this QROM Toffoli cost can be lowered to 2​32​N​D2\sqrt{32ND} while also using 32​N​D\sqrt{32ND} dirty qubits.

We also could have chosen to use SelSwapDirty QROM to flip the register |i⟩\left|i\right\rangle using |bi⟩\left|b_{i}\right\rangle in

∑i=1Dαi|i⟩|νi⟩v|bi⟩b,\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{D}\alpha_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left|\nu_{i}\right\rangle_{v}\left|b_{i}\right\rangle_{b}, (52)

where we have denoted the registers by subscripts. We need to employ the inverse O†O^{\dagger} of the SelSwapDirty operator O|bi⟩b|0⟩⊗log⁡D=|bi⟩b|i⟩O\left|b_{i}\right\rangle_{b}\left|0\right\rangle^{\otimes\log D}=\left|b_{i}\right\rangle_{b}\left|i\right\rangle. The naive implementation of OO would read 2​log⁡D−12\log D-1 qubits of bib_{i}, therefore its optimized Toffoli cost would scale as O⁡(D2⋅log⁡D)=O⁡(D​log⁡D)O(\sqrt{D^{2}\cdot\log D})=O(D\sqrt{\log D}). However, know that we only have D∼2log⁡DD\sim 2^{\log D} many bib_{i}’s and we would like to exploit this fact, achieving a Toffoli cost that is sublinear in DD.

First we note that we have knowledge of the value of bib_{i} as we computed them classically. Let λ=⌈D⌉\lambda=\lceil\sqrt{D}\rceil. Let us now order bl1<⋯<blDb_{l_{1}}<\cdots<b_{l_{D}}. We compute:

|bj⟩|0⟩⊗⌈log⁡D/2⌉→|bj⟩|f(j)⟩\displaystyle\left|b_{j}\right\rangle\left|0\right\rangle^{\otimes\lceil\log D/2\rceil}\to\left|b_{j}\right\rangle\left|f(j)\right\rangle (53)

where f⁡(j)f(j) is the unique index such that blλ⁡(f⁡(j)−1)<bj<blλ​f​(j)b_{l_{\lambda(f(j)-1)}}<b_{j}<b_{l_{\lambda f(j)}}, where for λ​f​(j)>D\lambda f(j)>D, we set iλ​f​(j)=Di_{\lambda f(j)}=D. This computation requires comparing bjb_{j} to ⌈D/λ⌉\lceil D/\lambda\rceil many other bib_{i}’s. This means a Toffoli cost of (2​log⁡D−1+2​log⁡D−1)(2\log D-1+2\log D-1) (the comparator cost of two 2​log⁡D−12\log D-1 bits integers) multiplied by the ⌈Dλ⌉\lceil\frac{D}{\lambda}\rceil comparisons that we have to make. More precisely, starting from bq​λb_{q\lambda} for q=1q=1, we compare bjb_{j} with bq​λb_{q\lambda} stored in an auxiliary register, and if bj>bq​λb_{j}>b_{q\lambda}, we store |1⟩\left|1\right\rangle in another auxiliary register and otherwise |0⟩\left|0\right\rangle. Then we add the value of that register to another register holding |q⟩\left|q\right\rangle which will eventually become |f(j)⟩\left|f(j)\right\rangle. This summation itself costs ⌈log⁡D/2⌉+1\lceil\log D/2\rceil+1 Toffolis as the size of the register holding qq is ⌈log⁡D/2⌉\lceil\log D/2\rceil (the qubit cost is effectively zero, as any ancilla used is immediately liberated without Toffolis). As this summation must be performed for all q∈{1,…,⌈Dλ⌉}q\in\{1,\ldots,\lceil\frac{D}{\lambda}\rceil\}, we have an additional ⌈log⁡D/2⌉⋅⌈Dλ⌉\lceil\log D/2\rceil\cdot\lceil\frac{D}{\lambda}\rceil to account for. In total, the cost for this computation is (4​log⁡D−2+⌈log⁡D/2⌉)​⌈Dλ⌉∼9​log⁡D​D2(4\log D-2+\lceil\log D/2\rceil)\lceil\frac{D}{\lambda}\rceil\sim\frac{9\log D\sqrt{D}}{2}, and we note that its (later) uncomputation can be done with Clifford gates. After this, our state becomes

∑i=1Dαi|i⟩|νi⟩v|bi⟩b|f(i)⟩\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{D}\alpha_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left|\nu_{i}\right\rangle_{v}\left|b_{i}\right\rangle_{b}\left|f(i)\right\rangle (54)

Next, we read the register f⁡(i)f(i) using a Select QROM with cost 2log⁡D/22^{\log D/2} and output the λ\lambda-block of bjb_{j}’s in which we know bib_{i} lives in, i.e. : |blλ⁡(f⁡(j)−1)+1,…,blλ​f​(j)⟩\left|b_{l_{\lambda(f(j)-1)}+1},\ldots,b_{l_{\lambda f(j)}}\right\rangle.

∑i=1Dαi|i⟩|νi⟩v|bi⟩b|f(i)⟩|blλ⁡(f⁡(i)−1)+1,…,blλ​f​(i)⟩\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{D}\alpha_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left|\nu_{i}\right\rangle_{v}\left|b_{i}\right\rangle_{b}\left|f(i)\right\rangle\left|b_{l_{\lambda(f(i)-1)}+1},\ldots,b_{l_{\lambda f(i)}}\right\rangle (55)

Notice the significant clean qubit cost (2​log⁡D−1)​λ∼(2​log⁡D−1)​D(2\log D-1)\lambda\sim(2\log D-1)\sqrt{D}. The uncomputation of this step is later done with Clifford gates. CNOT-ing the register bib_{i} into the block yields:

∑i=1D\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{D} αi|i⟩|νi⟩v|bi⟩b|f(i)⟩⊗\displaystyle\alpha_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left|\nu_{i}\right\rangle_{v}\left|b_{i}\right\rangle_{b}\left|f(i)\right\rangle\otimes
|blλ⁡(f⁡(i)−1)+1⊕bi,…,blλ​f​(i)⊕bi⟩\displaystyle\left|b_{l_{\lambda(f(i)-1)}+1}\oplus b_{i},\ldots,b_{l_{\lambda f(i)}}\oplus b_{i}\right\rangle (56)

By using λ\lambda many (2​log⁡D−1)(2\log D-1)-MCCNOTs, with total Toffoli cost (2​log⁡D−1)​λ(2\log D-1)\lambda, we compute the index 1≤g⁡(i)≤λ1\leq g(i)\leq\lambda for which blλ⁡(f⁡(i)−1)+g⁡(i)=bib_{l_{\lambda(f(i)-1)+g(i)}}=b_{i}. More precisely, we hold in an auxiliary register the index |k⟩\left|k\right\rangle at which we are implementing the MCCNOT, and using Toffolis, bit by bit for every ⌈log⁡D2⌉\lceil\frac{\log D}{2}\rceil bits, add that to the register designed for holding g⁡(i)g(i) controlled on the result of the (2​log⁡D−1)(2\log D-1)-MCCNOT. This requires an additional ⌈log⁡D/2⌉\lceil\log D/2\rceil Toffolis and ensures that only the true k=g⁡(i)k=g(i) is added to the register designed for holding g⁡(i)g(i). Therefore, the total Toffoli cost of this step is (2​log⁡D+⌈log⁡D/2⌉−1)​λ∼5​log⁡D​D2(2\log D+\lceil\log D/2\rceil-1)\lambda\sim\frac{5\log D\sqrt{D}}{2}. We now have the following state

∑i=1D\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{D} αi|i⟩|νi⟩v|bi⟩b|f(i)⟩⊗\displaystyle\alpha_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left|\nu_{i}\right\rangle_{v}\left|b_{i}\right\rangle_{b}\left|f(i)\right\rangle\otimes
|blλ⁡(f⁡(i)−1)+1⊕bi,…,blλ​f​(i)⊕bi⟩|g(i)⟩\displaystyle\left|b_{l_{\lambda(f(i)-1)}+1}\oplus b_{i},\ldots,b_{l_{\lambda f(i)}}\oplus b_{i}\right\rangle\left|g(i)\right\rangle (57)

Notice the register |f(i),g(i)⟩\left|f(i),g(i)\right\rangle has 2​⌈log⁡D2⌉∼log⁡D2\lceil\frac{\log D}{2}\rceil\sim\log D qubits, and determines ii uniquely. Tracing this back to our original goal of distinguishing the DD many νi\nu_{i}’s, this is the ideal we can hope for, as we have computed DD many log⁡(D)\log(D)-bits integers |f(i),g(i)⟩\left|f(i),g(i)\right\rangle that are distinct. The rest can be done using the inverse O†O^{\dagger} of a SelSwapDirty QROM which computes

O|f(i),g(i)⟩|0⟩⊗log⁡D=|f(i),g(i)⟩|i⟩\displaystyle O\left|f(i),g(i)\right\rangle\left|0\right\rangle^{\otimes\log D}=\left|f(i),g(i)\right\rangle\left|i\right\rangle (58)

Notice that we have access to where bib_{i} is in the list bl1<…<blDb_{l_{1}}<\ldots<b_{l_{D}}, and therefore can classically compute the values f⁡(i),g⁡(i)f(i),g(i). Hence the QROM has the required classical lookup data. This SelSwapDirty QROM has Toffoli cost 2​16​log⁡(D)​2log⁡D<2​32​log⁡(D)​D2\sqrt{16\log(D)2^{\log D}}<2\sqrt{32\log(D)D} with dirty qubit cost <32​log⁡(D)​D<\sqrt{32\log(D)D}. Note that these dirty qubits are already available using the λ−\lambda-block which has (2​log⁡D−1)​D(2\log D-1)\sqrt{D} qubits.

Resource estimation. Overall, the clean qubit cost increases to (2​log⁡D−1)​D(2\log D-1)\sqrt{D}, and an additional dirty qubit cost 32​N​D\sqrt{32ND}. The clean qubit cost may be improved if one can find a way to compute g⁡(i)g(i) without outputting the entire λ−\lambda-block. While the dirty qubit cost can be avoided if we do not apply SelSwapDirty QROM in Eq. 10. In practice, the dirty qubit cost, though significantly larger than the clean (5​log⁡D5\log D) qubit cost in our previous method, may be actually available if a future computation (such as qubitization) to simulate the evolution of the Hamiltonian requires that much qubit. The Toffoli cost changes to min⁡(2​32​N​D,D)+9​log⁡D​D2+5​log⁡D​D2+2log⁡D/2+2​32​l​o​g​(D)​D∼min⁡(2​32​N​D,D)+(7​log​D+2​32​log⁡D)​D\min(2\sqrt{32ND},D)+\frac{9\log D\sqrt{D}}{2}+\frac{5\log D\sqrt{D}}{2}+2^{\log D/2}+2\sqrt{32log(D)D}\sim\min(2\sqrt{32ND},D)+(7\log D+2\sqrt{32\log D})\sqrt{D}. In case DD is chosen from the minimum, the dirty qubit cost 32​N​D\sqrt{32ND} is lifted.

Is the algorithm optimal? Our algorithm is general in the sense that it simply assumes a given set of amplitudes {αi}\{\alpha_{i}\} and bitstrings {νi}\{\nu_{i}\}, with no assumption on the nature of either of the two sets. Furthermore, a dimensionality argument can show that the compression in Lemma III.1 of νi\nu_{i} to 2​log⁡D−12\log D-1 bits is very likely to be tight, and we conjecture that the volume cost can not be asymptotically lower than O~​(D)\tilde{O}(D), and more strongly, O⁡((log⁡D)2​D)O((\log D)^{2}D). We remark that this conjecture is for creating the superposition ∑i=1Dαi|νi⟩\sum_{i=1}^{D}\alpha_{i}\left|\nu_{i}\right\rangle, without any junk register, i.e. ∑i=1Dαi|νi⟩|junki⟩\sum_{i=1}^{D}\alpha_{i}\left|\nu_{i}\right\rangle\left|\text{junk}_{i}\right\rangle is not acceptable. The only ‘approximation’ allowed is in the amplitudes, and the distance to the state should be on the order of chemical accuracy. Both These restrictions are necessary as this preparation problem concerns the system register, and not, say, a PREP state in a qubitization protocol derived from an LCU, which can include a junk register, and hence why preparation methods such as coherent alias sampling [69] can be employed in that instance.

One wonders if the approach in [18] in iteratively generating the superposition can be combined with ours. This would involve ordering the states νi\nu_{i} and compressing ν1,…,νl\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{l} for each 1≤l≤D1\leq l\leq D. Assuming that for each ll, a compression of the bitstrings ν1,…,νl\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{l} to a length klk_{l} is possible (and we know kl≤2​⌈log⁡l⌉−1k_{l}\leq 2\lceil\log l\rceil-1), then the Toffoli cost of generating the superposition is ∑l=1D(kl−1)\sum_{l=1}^{D}(k_{l}-1). This is upper bounded by ∑i=1⌈log⁡D⌉−2(2​i−1)​(2i−1)+(2​⌈log⁡D⌉−1)​(D−2⌈log⁡D⌉−1)\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil\log D\rceil-2}(2i-1)(2^{i}-1)+(2\lceil\log D\rceil-1)(D-2^{\lceil\log D\rceil-1}) and can be seen to be smaller than our own cost (2​⌈log⁡D⌉+3)​D(2\lceil\log D\rceil+3)D. However, this method also involves a rotation at each step for 1≤l≤D1\leq l\leq D, and even assuming access to a gradient state, the overall cost of these rotations is (c−3)​D(c-3)D Toffolis, where cc is the required bit precision. Note that we also have to take into account the accuracy cc for our rotations in generating the superposition in Eq. 9, however the associated cost is simply (c−3)​log⁡D(c-3)\log D, and according to Lemma E.1 in [67], cc must satisfy c>log⁡(log⁡(D)​π/ϵ)c>\log(\log(D)\pi/\epsilon), where ϵ\epsilon is chemical accuracy. Crucially, cc is double logarithmic in terms of DD, because there are only log⁡D\log D rotations performed in generating Eq. 9. This is not the case when using the approach in [18], and for the overall error to be under chemical accuracy, we need c>log⁡(D​π/ϵ)c>\log(D\pi/\epsilon), therefore making cc logarithmic in DD. Still, one could see the total cost ∑i=1⌈log⁡D⌉−2(2​i−1)​(2i−1)+(2​⌈log⁡D⌉−1)​(D−2⌈log⁡D⌉−1)+(log⁡(D​π/ϵ)−3)​D\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil\log D\rceil-2}(2i-1)(2^{i}-1)+(2\lceil\log D\rceil-1)(D-2^{\lceil\log D\rceil-1})+(\log(D\pi/\epsilon)-3)D to be competitive within a constant factor of two with (2​⌈log⁡D⌉+3)​D(2\lceil\log D\rceil+3)D, but clearly, it does not lead to a significant constant factor cost reduction. Nevertheless, this is a worst case complexity analysis, and if klk_{l}’s are significantly smaller, one might see benefits of this combination of the two methods. This could potentially be the case for a particular range of DD and bitstrings νi\nu_{i}’s which have some common structure, such as being an excitation or two away from a reference state, and we leave that for future works.

Appendix E Details of resource estimation for MPS implementation

In this appendix we discuss the details of the MPS cost estimation presented in Sec. III.2. In particular we focus on the ancilla qubit and Toffoli costs of implementing G⁡[j]G[j] defined in Eq. 23.

We represent the GG operations as:

G[j]=∑αj−1(|uαj−1⟩⟨αj−1,0|)+…,G[j]=\sum_{\alpha_{j-1}}\left(\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle\left\langle\alpha_{j-1},0\right|\right)+\ldots, (59)

with

|uαj−1⟩=∑αj,njAj;αj−1​αjnj|αj,nj⟩.\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle=\sum_{\alpha_{j},n_{j}}A^{n_{j}}_{j;\ \alpha_{j-1}\alpha_{j}}\left|\alpha_{j},n_{j}\right\rangle. (60)

In the states |αj,nj⟩\left|\alpha_{j},n_{j}\right\rangle the first and second arguments show the ancillae and system qudit indices respectively. Note that the form of Eq. 59 follows from the defintion of GG in Eq. 23. Each unitary is synthesized using a series of Householder reflections with the addition of a single ancilla qubit as follows:

|0⟩⟨1|⊗G[j]+|1⟩⟨0|⊗G[j]†=∏αj−1=1χj−1(1−2Pαj−1)\left|0\right\rangle\left\langle 1\right|\otimes G[j]+\left|1\right\rangle\left\langle 0\right|\otimes G[j]^{\dagger}=\prod_{\alpha_{j-1}=1}^{\chi_{j-1}}(1-2P_{\alpha_{j-1}}) (61)

where a total of χj−1\chi_{j-1} reflections are used, whose projectors are defined through an auxiliary state |wαj−1⟩\left|w_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle:

Pαj−1=|wαj−1⟩⟨wαj−1|,P_{\alpha_{j-1}}=\left|w_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle\left\langle w_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right|, (62)

with

|wαj−1⟩\displaystyle\left|w_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle =|1⟩⊗|αj−1,0⟩−|0⟩⊗|uαj−1⟩\displaystyle=\left|1\right\rangle\otimes\left|\alpha_{j-1},0\right\rangle-\left|0\right\rangle\otimes\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle (63)
=Wαj−1|0⟩⊗|0,0⟩.\displaystyle=W_{\alpha_{j-1}}\left|0\right\rangle\otimes\left|0,0\right\rangle.

On the second row, we have defined the operator Wαj−1W_{\alpha_{j-1}} that prepares |wαj−1⟩\left|w_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle, also in the state |0⟩⊗|0,0⟩\left|0\right\rangle\otimes\left|0,0\right\rangle the 0’s correspond to the reflection ancilla, MPS ancillae and the system qudit respectively.

With the operator Wαj−1W_{\alpha_{j-1}}, each of the reflections in Eq. 61 can be written as:

1−2Pαj−1=Wαj−1[1−2|0,0,0⟩⟨0,0,0|]Wαj−1†,1-2P_{\alpha_{j-1}}=W_{\alpha_{j-1}}\,\left[1-2\left|0,0,0\right\rangle\left\langle 0,0,0\right|\right]\,W_{\alpha_{j-1}}^{\dagger}, (64)

and thus the cost of implementing each reflection is twice the cost of Wαj−1W_{\alpha_{j-1}} plus the cost of the simple reflection [1−2|0,0,0⟩⟨0,0,0|]\left[1-2\left|0,0,0\right\rangle\left\langle 0,0,0\right|\right]. As a result, we need to also evaluate the cost of Wαj−1W_{\alpha_{j-1}}, which we synthesize as follows: we first define an operator that prepares the state |uαj−1⟩\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle:

|uαj−1⟩=Vαj−1|0,0⟩.\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle=V_{\alpha_{j-1}}\left|0,0\right\rangle. (65)

It can be seen that Wαj−1W_{\alpha_{j-1}} as below can serve to satisfy the definition of |wαj−1⟩\left|w_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle in Eq. 63:

Wαj−1=(C¯​Vαj−1)​(Cαj−1)​((Z​H)⊗𝕀),W_{\alpha_{j-1}}=\left(\bar{C}V_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right)\left(C_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right)\left((ZH)\otimes\mathbb{I}\right), (66)

where Z​HZH (a Pauli ZZ and a Hadamard) acts on the reflection ancilla, Cαj−1C_{\alpha_{j-1}} is a product of CNOTs controlled on the reflection ancilla to prepare the state 12[|0,0,0⟩−|1,αj,0⟩]\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\left|0,0,0\right\rangle-\left|1,\alpha_{j},0\right\rangle\right]. With C¯​Vαj−1\bar{C}V_{\alpha_{j-1}} controlled negatively on the reflection ancilla, one can check that |wαj−1⟩\left|w_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle is prepared up to a phase.

We are interested in the Toffoli cost of implementation and list all sources of Toffoli cost below:

  • •

    Simple reflections [1−2|0,0,0⟩⟨0,0,0|]\left[1-2\left|0,0,0\right\rangle\left\langle 0,0,0\right|\right]: a number of χj−1\chi_{j-1} of them is required for G⁡[j]G[j].

  • •

    Operations C¯​Vαj−1\bar{C}V_{\alpha_{j-1}}: these are required for creating Wαj−1W_{\alpha_{j-1}} and are the only source of non-Clifford gates in their synthesis. A total of 2​χj−12\chi_{j-1} of such operators is required for G⁡[j]G[j].

First we note that the reflection [1−2|0⟩⊗ν⟨0|⊗ν]\left[1-2\left|0\right\rangle^{\otimes\nu}\left\langle 0\right|^{\otimes\nu}\right] can essentially be thought of as a multi-controlled Z operation, and thus can be implemented using a circuit such as the one shown in figure 4.10 of [11]. However, the second half of the circuit, i.e. the uncomputing part can be done without Toffolis and in fact using measurements and Clifford gates as shown in figure 3 of Ref. [86]. This makes the total number of Toffoli gates and ancillae equal to ν−1\nu-1.

Next, we discuss how C¯​Vαj−1\bar{C}V_{\alpha_{j-1}} can be implemented and estimate the required resources. For this we first discuss the implementation of Vαj−1V_{\alpha_{j-1}}. Vαj−1V_{\alpha_{j-1}} prepares the state:

|uαj−1⟩=Vαj−1|0,0⟩,\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle=V_{\alpha_{j-1}}\left|0,0\right\rangle, (67)

which is defined as:

|uαj−1⟩=∑αj,njAj;αj−1​αjnj|αj,nj⟩.\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle=\sum_{\alpha_{j},n_{j}}A^{n_{j}}_{j;\ \alpha_{j-1}\alpha_{j}}\left|\alpha_{j},n_{j}\right\rangle. (68)

First, we take the above subspace of interest to consist of ν\nu qubits. The preparation of a generic state as |uαj−1⟩\left|u_{\alpha_{j-1}}\right\rangle can be done using the methods discussed in Ref. [68]; the state is carved qubit by qubit in ν\nu steps; in each step a single qubit rotations on one qubit being controlled on all the previous entries is performed and with consecutive application of this procedure all the correct probabilities for bitstrings are reproduced at the end; one last multicontrolled single qubit rotation is required to recover the complex phases corresponding to the components of the state in question (see page 3 of [68] for details). Thus a total of ν+1\nu+1 of such single qubit rotations are required for reproducing the state.

The rotation will be performed with the method given in [86], where access to a phase gradient state 2−b/2∑k=02b−1e−2πik/2b|k⟩2^{-b/2}\sum_{k=0}^{2^{b}-1}e^{-2\pi ik/2^{b}}\left|k\right\rangle is assumed. b=log⁡(1/δr)b=\log(1/\delta_{r}) is the number of digits in the binary representation of the rotation angle and thus δr\delta_{r} is the error in rotation. The Toffoli cost of each single qubit rotation is given by b+O⁡(1)b+O(1) [86]; note that this also means we need an additional log⁡(1/δr)\log(1/\delta_{r}) additional qubits to store the phase of each single qubit rotation.

Considering first the Select variant of implementation in [68], we now discuss the cost of control operations for the above single qubit rotations. Since multicontrolling over a sequence of 0,1,2,…,ν0,1,2,\ldots,\nu qubits is required to store the respective rotation angles, we will respectively have a sequence of Toffoli costs of 20−1,21−1,22−1,…,2ν−12^{0}-1,2^{1}-1,2^{2}-1,\ldots,2^{\nu}-1 according to [87] (see e.g. figure 7 therein). Note that we are interested in implementing C¯​Vαj−1\bar{C}V_{\alpha_{j-1}}, and [87] also considers a controlled operation for the above cost. After each single qubit rotation, the qubits storing the rotation angle should be uncomputed and this adds a multiplicative factor of 2. As a result, for the Select variant we have a total Toffoli cost equal to

2ν+2+ν​b.2^{\nu+2}+\nu b. (69)

Where we have dropped an additive −ν-\nu term in the sum as it is subdominant.

In our particular case of interest, i.e. synthesis of G⁡[j]G[j], we have a number of reflections shown in Eq. 61, equal to χj−1\chi_{j-1}. On the other hand the Hilbert space over which each of the relections acts is χj​d\chi_{j}d and as a result, NN in the above trwatments should be 2ν=χj​d2^{\nu}=\chi_{j}d. This means that in the Select variant, the total Toffoli cost reads:

χj−1​[8​χj​d+b​log⁡(χj​d)+log⁡(χj​d)],\chi_{j-1}\left[8\chi_{j}d+b\log(\chi_{j}d)+\log(\chi_{j}d)\right], (70)

Next turning to the other variant SelSwapDirty of Ref. [68], which is capable of reducing the Toffoli cost if dirty qubits are available; we saw above that a number bb qubits is required for storing the rotation angles, however with the addition of a number λ​b\lambda b dirty qubits, we can use this variant of the algorithm. A total of ν+b\nu+b extra clean qubits are also required (excluding the ancillae required for performing single qubit rotations like the phase gradient state); note that this is the same number as the Select variant. Moreover, for SelSwapDirty, one needs to perform swaps also which will add to the total Toffoli cost. It is straightforward to see that the Toffoli gate cost in this case reads:

2​2ν+2λ+4⋅2​λ​ν​b+ν​b.2\frac{2^{\nu+2}}{\lambda}+4\cdot 2\lambda\nu b+\nu b. (71)

The first term corresponds to multi-qubit controls, the second term swaps and the third term single qubit rotations. The factors 2 and 4 in the first and the second terms appear because Select and Swap need to be done twice and four times in SelSwapDirty (See figure 1d of [68]). The factor of 2 in the second term comes from uncomputing the rotation angles.

As is discussed in [68], it is best for Toffoli gate count to be λ=O⁡(2ν)\lambda=O(\sqrt{2^{\nu}}), but we will keep it unspecified for the rest of the discussion.

Gathering all the above costs together for synthesizing G⁡[j]G[j] in Eq. 59, we see that the Toffoli cost reads using the SelSwapDirty variant:

χj−1​[8​χj​dλ+8​λ​b​log⁡(χj​d)+b​log⁡(χj​d)+log⁡(χj​d)]\chi_{j-1}\left[8\frac{\chi_{j}d}{\lambda}+8\lambda b\log(\chi_{j}d)+b\log(\chi_{j}d)+\log(\chi_{j}d)\right] (72)

In total assuming a number NN of qudits in the physical system, the total cost will be the sum of the above; asymptotically and with using χ\chi selctively for all bond dimensions, the dominant Toffoli cost can be written as O⁡(N​χ3/2)O(N\chi^{3/2}).

Appendix G Kernel density approximation

Here, we give a quick overview of the kernel density approximation method. Supposing we have access to a finite number of samples drawn from a distribution function, the goal is to approximate the distribution function. To this end, a broadening kernel is placed at the position of each of the outcomes and a normalized sum approximates the underlying distribution:

p^​(x)=1M​h​∑i=1MK⁡(x−Xih),\hat{p}(x)=\frac{1}{Mh}\sum_{i=1}^{M}K\left(\frac{x-X_{i}}{h}\right), (75)

where KK is a kernel (e.g. Gaussian, Lorentzian, etc.) with mean of 0 and variance of 1, Xi,i=1,…,MX_{i},i=1,\ldots,M are the outcomes of sampling and hh is the broadening factor.

The analysis of error in reconstructing the above QPE-kernel energy distribution with kernel density estimation follows a standard approach [79]. First, the error is quantified by the quantity mean integrated square error (MISE):

MISE=𝔼⁡(∫d​x​(p^​(x)−p⁡(x))2),\text{MISE}=\mathbb{E}\left(\int dx\;(\hat{p}(x)-p(x))^{2}\right), (76)

where p^​(x)\hat{p}(x) is the approximated distribution for the underlying distribution p⁡(x)p(x). When a sample of size MM is used, it is well known that with an appropriate choice of hh, i.e. hopt∼1/M1/5h_{\text{opt}}\sim 1/M^{1/5}, the error also shows the behavior MISE∼1/M4/5\text{MISE}\sim 1/M^{4/5}.

Appendix H Details of the quantum eigenvalue transformation of unitary matrices method

The method consists of a quantum signal processing circuit [82, 83] that implements a unitary matrix that block encodes a polynomial function f⁡(H)=P⁡(cos⁡(H/2))f(H)=P(\cos(H/2)), where HH is the Hamiltonian of interest and PP is an even polynomial of degree dd. A schematic of the quantum circuit is shown in Fig. 16. The circuit works by implementing U=e−i​HU=e^{-iH} and its Hermitian conjugate controlled on a single ancilla, a total number of dd times. The parameters φ0,φ1,…,φd/2\varphi_{0},\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{d/2} are determined based on the polynomial of interest. Upon measuring the ancilla qubit at the end and obtaining the outcome 00, the implementation has been successful, the probability of success is given by ∥P(cos(H/2))|ψ⟩∥\|P(\cos(H/2))\left|\psi\right\rangle\|.

A scheme of the quantum circuit is shown in Fig. 16. The circuit works by implementing U=e−i​HU=e^{-iH} and its Hermitian conjugate controlled on a single ancilla, a total number of dd times. The parameters φ0,φ1,…,φd/2\varphi_{0},\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{d/2} are determined based on the polynomial of interest. Upon measuring the ancilla qubit at the end and obtaining the outcome 00, the implementation has been successful, the probability of success is given by ∥P(cos(H/2))|ψ⟩∥\|P(\cos(H/2))\left|\psi\right\rangle\|.

The polynomial that needs to be implemented for our energy filtering task should be a symmetric function that retains low energies and filters high energies. We take the spectrum of the Hamiltonian to lie within the interval [−π+η,0−η][-\pi+\eta,0-\eta], if necessary this can be done by adding a constant to and/or rescaling the Hamiltonian before performing QETU. Note that this is contrary to the original setting of Ref. [81] (the spectrum is contained in [η,π−η][\eta,\pi-\eta]) and coarse QPE mentioned above; the reason for this change is better performance. We need a polynomial PP which when expressed as P⁡(cos⁡(H/2))P(\cos(H/2)) can filter high energies; it is straightforward to see that using the following combination of error functions, which we will try to imitate using the polynomial PP, it is possible to filter high energies:

ξk,μ​(x)=12​[erf⁡(−k⁡(x−μ))+erf⁡(k⁡(x+μ))],\xi_{k,\mu}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathrm{erf}(-k(x-\mu))+\mathrm{erf}(k(x+\mu))\right], (77)

with 0<k0<k and 0<μ<10<\mu<1 determining the steepness and position of the transitions, i.e. position of energy filtering in the function. We use the prescription in Appendix A of Ref. [88] to reconstruct the error function erf⁡(k​x)\mathrm{erf}(kx) in terms of Chebyshev polynomials as follows:

perf,k,n\displaystyle p_{\text{erf},k,n} =2ke−k2/2π​(I0​(k2/2)CLOSE\displaystyle=\frac{2k\,e^{-k^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg(I_{0}(k^{2}/2) (78)
+∑j=1(n−1)/2\displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{(n-1)/2} OPEN(−1)j​Ij​(k2/2)​[T2​j+1​(x)2​j+1−T2​j−1​(x)2​j−1]),\displaystyle(-1)^{j}I_{j}(k^{2}/2)\left[\frac{T_{2j+1}(x)}{2j+1}-\frac{T_{2j-1}(x)}{2j-1}\right]\bigg),

where TjT_{j} is the degree jj Chebyshev polynomial, IjI_{j} is the modified Bessel function of the first kind. Note that perf,k,np_{\text{erf},k,n} is an odd polynomial of degree nn; it is the degree nn that controls the error in approximating erf⁡(k​x)\mathrm{erf}(kx) and thus ensuring that low energies are retained and high energies filtered, and therefore it should be chosen large enough (see below). An example constructing polynomials like this is shown in Fig. 17.

Applying a successful round of QETU filtering to a state |ψ⟩=∑EφE|E⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{E}\varphi_{E}\left|E\right\rangle, we end up with the following unnormalized state:

∑EφEP(cos(E/2))|E⟩|0⟩,\sum_{E}\varphi_{E}\,P(\cos(E/2))\left|E\right\rangle\left|0\right\rangle, (79)

This shows that supposing we want to keep energies below ElE_{l} and filter energies above EuE_{u}, we can choose a filtering function in Eq. 77 (to be approximated by PP) with μ=cos⁡(Eu/2)+cos⁡(El/2)2\mu=\frac{\cos(E_{u}/2)+\cos(E_{l}/2)}{2} and 1k=ζ​cos⁡(Eu/2)−cos⁡(El/2)2\frac{1}{k}=\zeta\,\frac{\cos(E_{u}/2)-\cos(E_{l}/2)}{2}. The factor ζ\zeta is added so that it is possible to control the intensity of filtering while keeping the degree of the polynomial and the cost down.

The degree of a polynomial that needs to be used for this task will have a scaling O⁡(Γ−1​log⁡ϵ−1)O(\Gamma^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1}), where ϵ\epsilon is the error in the polynomial approximation and Γ\Gamma is the energy scale over which the transition in the error functions in Eq. 77 happens, and thus should scale as 1/k1/k. Apart form the above asymptotic scaling, in practice, we choose nn by examining how good of an approximation is achieved for degree nn.

Appendix I Simplified numerical example for the quantum refining step

Here, as a simple concrete model, we consider a Gaussian energy distribution for our initial state. This Gaussian distribution can be characterized by a mean value E¯\bar{E} and a width σE\sigma_{E}:

A⁡(E)=12​π​σE​e−(E−E¯)22​σE2,A(E)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_{E}}\ e^{-\frac{(E-\bar{E})^{2}}{2\sigma_{E}^{2}}}, (80)

Even though the energy distribution of an initial state might not actually be close to Gaussian in general, but we expect at least some variational states to show qualitatively similar behavior.

We work with following concrete example of a Gaussian distribution: E¯=0.06,σ=0.02\bar{E}=0.06,\,\sigma=0.02. We would like to estimate the resources required to obtain a result close to 0 using QPE. With the above choice of parameters for the energy distribution, the accumulated weight below 0 is p<​(0)=0.0013p_{<}(0)=0.0013. This means that we need roughly 1/p<​(0)1/p_{<}(0) measurements to obtain a value around 0. We can perform quantum refining to decrease the number of times the most expensive quantum energy estimation routine is performed. We take this most precise routine to be a QPE with k=10k=10 digits for this example, however, we tolerate an error of 2−82^{-8}, discarding the last two digits in any QPE outcome. The number of digits kk furthermore determines the total evolution time required as T∼2kT\sim 2^{k}. We characterize the cost of different operations by the number of queries they require to the unitary e−i​He^{-iH}, which for a kk-digit QPE measurement becomes 2k2^{k}. This means that each round of the ultimate QPE measurement brings in a cost of 2102^{10}.

We first consider coarse QPE for energy filtering in this setting. Concretely, we do a coarse QPE measurement with 4 digits and only keep the results that show outcome 0 in the measured phase register, we can filter out some part of the weight as shown in Fig. 7 (left). This outcome happens with a probability of Wk=4=0.10W_{k=4}=0.10. In this new energy distribution the total weight below zero now reads pQPE,<′​(0)=0.012p^{\prime}_{\text{QPE},<}(0)=0.012. This means that, after such measurement, roughly ten times less rounds of the precision QPE will be required compared to the initial state.

One can do this procedure one more time with a coarse QPE with 5 digits now and postselecting on the outcome 0 again; the resulting weight distribution can be seen in Fig. 7 (left). The probability of such outcome (given the previous outcome of 0 with 4 digits) is now Wk=4;5=0.13W_{k=4;5}=0.13 (this means that the probability of obtaining 0 in the 4-digit measurement and then also 0 in the 5-digits measurement is Wk=4​Wk=4;5=0.013W_{k=4}W_{k=4;5}=0.013). Remarkably with this measurement, the total weight below zero becomes pQPE,<′′​(0)=0.083p^{\prime\prime}_{\text{QPE},<}(0)=0.083; this results in close to two orders of magnitude decrease in the number of precision QPE measurement required for obtaining outcomes close to 0. This is achieved for a cost of 24+252^{4}+2^{5} which is an insignificant overhead compared with the cost of the most precise QPE measurement.

For QETU, we shift the energies so that low energies are located close to −π-\pi as discussed in Appendix H. We use a degree 200 polynomial to approximate a step function as shown in Fig. 7. The normalized distribution after QETU has been performed moves to the left and thus some of the higher energies are filtered. Probability of success in this case is WQETU=0.21W_{\text{QETU}}=0.21 and the total weight below 0 after the procedure can also be calculated as pQETU,<′=0.0056p^{\prime}_{\text{QETU},<}=0.0056. This means decreasing the number of repetitions roughly by a factor of 4. As the polynomial that is used is order 200, the number of required queries to e−i​He^{-iH} is also 200.

We see that both coarse QPE and QETU refining methods can be helpful for a cost that is an insignificant fraction of the ultimate QPE cost, but coarse QPE acts considerably better for a lower cost. As creating steep polynomials like the one used here is generally a hard task, we believe this result should hold generically even though we tested it here for a simple model.

I.0.1 Mitigating the leakage

Another thing which can be studied in this simple model is the probability of leakage before and after the refining is performed. We only consider coarse QPE for this. Before any of the measurements are performed the total probability of leakage is equal to pleak=0.00097p_{\text{leak}}=0.00097 which close to p<​(0)=0.0013p_{<}(0)=0.0013 and this can be problematic by contributing outcomes below the actual energy levels of th system. Upon performing 4-digit and 5-digit QPE measurements discussed above, the probability of leakage become pleak′=0.0019p^{\prime}_{\text{leak}}=0.0019 and respectively pleak′′=0.0036p^{\prime\prime}_{\text{leak}}=0.0036. These two values when compared with pQPE,<′​(0)=0.012p^{\prime}_{\text{QPE},<}(0)=0.012 and pQPE,<′′​(0)=0.083p^{\prime\prime}_{\text{QPE},<}(0)=0.083 show that the probability of leakage has decreased substantially enough compared to the probability of obtaining results of interest, so that its occurrence has become improbable, and thus quantum refining has suppressed the possibility of leakage also.

Appendix J Error analysis of the QPE leakage approximate form

In this appendix we analyze Eq. 45 and in particular how the approximation in Eq. 46 can be performed.

pleak​(En)=∑xj<xupper122​k​(sin2⁡(π​δn)sin2⁡(π2k​[xn+δn−xj])),p_{\text{leak}}(E_{n})=\sum_{x_{j}<x_{\text{upper}}}\frac{1}{2^{2k}}\left(\frac{\sin^{2}(\pi\delta_{n})}{\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2^{k}}[x_{n}+\delta_{n}-x_{j}]\right)}\right), (81)

we take the lower bound in the summation over xjx_{j} to be −2k−1-2^{k-1}, and we are using the periodicity of the QPE results. A lower bound and an upper bound for the above sum can be found by using the following integral form:

I⁡(x0)\displaystyle I(x_{0}) =sin2⁡(π​δn)22​k​∫−2k−1x0d​xsin2⁡(π2k​(xn+δn−x))\displaystyle=\frac{\sin^{2}(\pi\delta_{n})}{2^{2k}}\,\int_{-2^{k-1}}^{x_{0}}\frac{dx}{\sin^{2}(\frac{\pi}{2^{k}}(x_{n}+\delta_{n}-x))} (82)
=sin2⁡(π​δn)22​k​[2kπ​cot⁡(π2k​(xn+δn−x))|−2k−1x0].\displaystyle=\frac{\sin^{2}(\pi\delta_{n})}{2^{2k}}\left[\left.\frac{2^{k}}{\pi}\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2^{k}}(x_{n}+\delta_{n}-x)\right)\right|^{x_{0}}_{-2^{k-1}}\right].

It is easy to check that:

I⁡(xupper−1)≤pleak​(En)≤I⁡(xupper).I(x_{\text{upper}}-1)\leq p_{\text{leak}}(E_{n})\leq I(x_{\text{upper}}). (83)

This readily results in Eq. 46, and the error can also be shown to have the form O⁡(max⁡[2−2​k,(xn−xupper)−2])O\left(\max\left[2^{-2k},(x_{n}-x_{\text{upper}})^{-2}\right]\right) by evaluating I⁡(xupper)−I⁡(xupper−1)I(x_{\text{upper}})-I(x_{\text{upper}}-1).
